column1: # subject :: doctrine :: application scenario :: concise correct rule

Civil Procedure::Diversity jurisdiction::A New York citizen sues a New Jersey citizen for $90,000 on a state-law contract claim in federal court. Which doctrine supports jurisdiction?::Complete diversity and more than $75,000 in controversy ordinarily support federal diversity jurisdiction.

Civil Procedure::Complete diversity::An Ohio plaintiff sues defendants from Ohio and Michigan on a state tort claim. Which doctrine defeats diversity?::No plaintiff may share state citizenship with any opposing defendant for complete diversity.

Civil Procedure::Well-pleaded complaint rule::A state-law negligence complaint merely anticipates a federal statutory defense. What rule prevents federal-question jurisdiction?::A federal question normally must appear on the face of the plaintiff's properly pleaded claim, not merely in a defense.

Civil Procedure::Removal deadline::A defendant receives a pleading first showing the case is removable and wants federal court. Which timing rule governs?::The ordinary deadline to remove is 30 days after receiving the pleading that first establishes removability.

Civil Procedure::Forum-defendant rule::A Texas defendant is sued in Texas state court and removal would rest solely on diversity. What rule normally blocks removal?::A properly joined and served forum-state defendant ordinarily cannot remove on diversity grounds alone.

Civil Procedure::Supplemental jurisdiction::A state negligence claim and a federal civil-rights claim arise from the same encounter. What allows both in federal court?::Related claims sharing a common nucleus of operative fact may be heard under supplemental jurisdiction.

Civil Procedure::Erie and Hanna doctrine::A valid Federal Rule directly controls a procedure in a diversity case despite different state procedure. Which doctrine governs?::A valid on-point Federal Rule generally applies in federal court, including diversity cases.

Civil Procedure::Specific personal jurisdiction::A seller purposefully targets a state's residents and is sued about a sale there. Which kind of jurisdiction is relevant?::Specific jurisdiction generally requires purposeful forum contacts related to the lawsuit and fairness.

Civil Procedure::General personal jurisdiction::An individual is permanently domiciled in Oregon but briefly visits Nevada. Which theory permits unrelated claims in Oregon?::Individuals are generally subject to general personal jurisdiction in their state of domicile.

Civil Procedure::Service deadline::A plaintiff files a federal complaint but does not serve the defendant for 90 days. What rule is implicated?::Rule 4(m) generally calls for service within 90 days, subject to exceptions and extensions.

Civil Procedure::Venue based on events::A substantial portion of the events occurred in a particular federal district. What makes venue proper there?::Venue may lie where a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claim occurred.

Civil Procedure::Section 1404 transfer::Witnesses and documents are located in another district where the case could have been filed. Which procedure fits?::A court may transfer venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) for convenience and in the interest of justice.

Civil Procedure::Claim preclusion::Parties try to relitigate the same claim after a valid final judgment on the merits. What bars the case?::Claim preclusion generally bars the same claim between the same parties or privies after a valid final merits judgment.

Civil Procedure::Issue preclusion::An essential factual issue was actually litigated and decided in a prior valid judgment. What doctrine bars relitigation?::Issue preclusion may bar an issue actually litigated, necessarily decided, and essential to a prior valid final judgment.

Civil Procedure::Summary judgment::After discovery, no genuine dispute of material fact remains and one side is entitled to judgment as law. Which motion fits?::Rule 56 allows summary judgment when no genuine dispute of material fact exists and movant wins as a matter of law.

Civil Procedure::Plausibility pleading::A complaint offers only labels and conclusions about negligence, without supporting facts. What pleading standard applies?::Rule 12(b)(6) requires sufficient factual allegations to make a claim plausible, not mere legal conclusions.

Civil Procedure::Personal jurisdiction waiver::A defendant omits a personal-jurisdiction objection from the first Rule 12 motion. What rule is implicated?::A personal-jurisdiction defense is generally waived if omitted from the required initial Rule 12 response.

Civil Procedure::Compulsory counterclaim::A defendant's claim against the plaintiff arises from the same transaction as the lawsuit. What is it called?::Rule 13(a) generally requires a counterclaim arising from the same transaction or occurrence, subject to exceptions.

Civil Procedure::Work-product protection::A lawyer writes litigation strategy notes in anticipation of a lawsuit. What doctrine protects the notes?::Materials prepared in anticipation of litigation receive qualified protection, with special protection for mental impressions.

Civil Procedure::Class numerosity::Hundreds of dispersed people share a common grievance, making joinder impracticable. Which Rule 23 requirement is shown?::Numerosity requires a sufficiently numerous class that joining all members is impracticable.

Constitutional Law::State action doctrine::A private shop excludes a customer for a political view without any governmental involvement. What limits a constitutional free-speech claim?::Many constitutional rights constrain government conduct rather than purely private action.

Constitutional Law::Commerce Clause aggregation::Congress regulates homegrown wheat as part of a broader interstate wheat market regulation. Which power supports it?::Congress may regulate local economic activity whose aggregate effect substantially affects interstate commerce.

Constitutional Law::Dormant Commerce Clause discrimination::A state taxes imported products more heavily than identical local products. What issue arises?::Facially discriminatory state laws burdening interstate commerce receive especially demanding review.

Constitutional Law::Spending Clause conditions::Congress offers transportation grants if states adopt related safety rules. Which power permits encouragement?::Congress may attach clear, related, noncoercive conditions to federal spending, within constitutional limits.

Constitutional Law::Anti-commandeering principle::Congress commands state legislatures to enact a federal program. What constitutional limit applies?::Congress ordinarily may not directly command state governments to legislate or administer federal programs.

Constitutional Law::Strict scrutiny for race::A public university classifies students explicitly by race. Which equal-protection standard applies?::Government racial classifications face strict scrutiny requiring a compelling interest and narrow tailoring.

Constitutional Law::Intermediate scrutiny for sex::A state uses different permit rules for men and women. Which review standard generally applies?::Sex-based classifications ordinarily require an important governmental objective and a substantial relationship.

Constitutional Law::Rational-basis review::A state creates an ordinary business licensing category not affecting suspect classes or fundamental rights. Which standard applies?::Ordinary economic regulation generally needs a rational relation to a legitimate government purpose.

Constitutional Law::Right to interstate travel::A state withholds basic newcomer benefits solely because residents recently moved from another state. What right is implicated?::The constitutional right to interstate travel protects movement and equal treatment of new residents.

Constitutional Law::Procedural due process::A public worker with a protected employment interest is fired without meaningful notice or opportunity to respond. What doctrine applies?::Government deprivation of protected life, liberty, or property interests ordinarily requires constitutionally appropriate process.

Constitutional Law::Viewpoint discrimination::A city allows pro-mayor protests but bans anti-mayor protests in the same public park. Which speech restriction is involved?::Government may not ordinarily favor a viewpoint over its opposing viewpoint in a public forum.

Constitutional Law::Content-based speech restriction::A city bans signs specifically criticizing a named public policy. What First Amendment framework applies?::Content-based speech regulations generally receive strict scrutiny unless an established exception applies.

Constitutional Law::Time-place-manner regulation::A city limits nighttime noise in public parks without regard to a speaker's message. Which doctrine applies?::Content-neutral time, place, and manner limits must be appropriately tailored and leave adequate alternatives.

Constitutional Law::Incitement standard::A speaker advocates unspecified future lawbreaking but not imminent action. What doctrine protects the speech?::Unprotected incitement requires advocacy intended and likely to produce imminent lawless action.

Constitutional Law::True threats::A speaker seriously communicates intent to inflict unlawful physical violence on an identified person. What speech category applies?::True threats constitute a limited category of speech that may be punished within constitutional requirements.

Constitutional Law::Free Exercise neutral law::A neutral, generally applicable safety law incidentally burdens a person's religious practice. What principle generally applies?::Neutral, generally applicable laws usually do not violate Free Exercise merely because they incidentally burden religion.

Constitutional Law::Takings Clause::Government takes a parcel for a public road with payment of fair compensation. What clause applies?::The Fifth Amendment Takings Clause requires public use and just compensation for covered government takings.

Constitutional Law::Supremacy Clause preemption::A valid federal statute directly conflicts with a state law. What principle resolves the conflict?::Valid federal law displaces conflicting state law under the Supremacy Clause.

Constitutional Law::Article III standing::A person sues over a policy but alleges no concrete personal harm. Which requirement is missing?::Federal standing generally requires injury in fact, causation, and likely redressability.

Constitutional Law::Ex post facto prohibition::A state criminalizes conduct that was lawful when committed and prosecutes it retroactively. Which constitutional bar applies?::The Ex Post Facto Clauses prohibit certain retroactive criminal laws, including criminalizing previously lawful conduct.

Contracts::Offer::A seller says 'I will sell this bike for $400 if you accept Friday,' intending acceptance to bind both sides. What is this?::An offer manifests willingness to bargain so the offeree's assent concludes the agreement.

Contracts::Counteroffer::A buyer replies to a common-law land-sale offer, 'I agree if you also include the furniture.' What is the reply?::Under the common-law mirror-image rule, a material change normally makes the response a counteroffer.

Contracts::UCC battle of the forms::Merchants exchange goods-contract forms, and the acceptance includes an additional term without expressly conditioning assent. Which rule governs?::UCC 2-207 permits a definite acceptance despite additional or different terms, with special rules for their inclusion.

Contracts::Consideration::A painter agrees to paint a house and the owner agrees to pay an agreed sum. What makes the promises enforceable?::Consideration is a bargained-for exchange of legal value or promises.

Contracts::Past consideration::A neighbor promises cash as thanks for a favor already completed with no prior arrangement. What obstacle exists?::Past services generally are not consideration for a subsequent promise.

Contracts::Promissory estoppel::An employer makes a clear job promise, inducing a candidate to move at substantial expense before withdrawing it. What remedy theory fits?::Reasonable, foreseeable reliance on a promise may support relief when needed to avoid injustice.

Contracts::Minor's contractual capacity::A 16-year-old timely disaffirms a non-necessaries purchase contract. Which defense applies?::A minor's contract for non-necessaries is generally voidable at the minor's option, subject to exceptions.

Contracts::Duress::Someone signs a deal only because the other side credibly threatens unlawful violence. Which defense applies?::Improper threats that leave no reasonable alternative may make an agreement voidable for duress.

Contracts::Mutual mistake::Both parties wrongly believe a painting is an original, a basic assumption critical to the sale. Which doctrine applies?::Material mutual mistake about a basic assumption may permit avoidance if the complaining party did not bear the risk.

Contracts::Statute of frauds for land::Parties orally agree to transfer a parcel of land next month. Which formal requirement applies?::Contracts to convey interests in land ordinarily require a sufficient signed writing or a recognized exception.

Contracts::UCC statute of frauds::Two parties orally contract for $2,500 of goods without satisfying an exception. Which rule is relevant?::UCC 2-201 generally requires a sufficient signed writing for sales of goods priced at $500 or more.

Contracts::Parol evidence rule::A complete final written contract is contradicted by evidence of a prior oral promise. What rule may exclude the oral term?::Prior or contemporaneous agreements ordinarily cannot contradict a complete integrated writing.

Contracts::Condition precedent::A land contract makes bank approval necessary before a buyer must close. What type of contract term is approval?::A condition precedent is an event that must occur before an affected performance duty becomes due.

Contracts::Substantial performance::A builder completes a house with a minor nonmaterial defect and seeks payment less the cost to fix it. Which principle applies?::Substantial performance may allow contract recovery despite a minor breach, subject to an offset for defects.

Contracts::Anticipatory repudiation::A seller unequivocally announces before the delivery date that no goods will be shipped. What doctrine applies?::A clear advance refusal to perform can constitute anticipatory repudiation with resulting remedies.

Contracts::Perfect tender::A one-time shipment of goods does not conform to the contract description. Which UCC buyer remedy principle applies?::For many single-delivery sales, the buyer may reject a nonconforming tender, subject to cure and exceptions.

Contracts::Right to cure::A seller ships a wrong item before the contract deadline and offers the correct item before that date. What UCC right applies?::A seller generally may cure a defective tender within the agreed time for performance.

Contracts::Expectation damages::The injured buyer seeks the value of the promised performance rather than what was delivered. What measure applies?::Expectation damages aim to put the injured party in the position performance would have produced.

Contracts::Consequential-damages foreseeability::A carrier knows at contracting that late delivery will halt an unusual production line. Which damages limitation matters?::Unusual consequential contract losses generally must have been foreseeable when the contract was formed.

Contracts::Specific performance of land::A seller breaches an agreement to convey a unique parcel. Which remedy may a court grant?::Specific performance may be available where monetary damages are inadequate, especially for land.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Criminal attempt::A person intends a robbery and takes a substantial step but is stopped before taking property. What crime is established?::Attempt generally requires intent to commit the target offense and a substantial step toward it.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Solicitation::A person intentionally asks another to commit burglary, but the other refuses. What crime can already be complete?::Solicitation generally is completed by intentionally requesting or encouraging another to commit crime.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Conspiracy::Two people agree and intend to commit a felony, with an overt act where required. Which offense exists?::Conspiracy generally requires an agreement and intent to pursue unlawful conduct, sometimes with an overt act.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Accomplice liability::A lookout intentionally aids a planned robbery knowing and intending it to succeed. What theory applies?::An accomplice intentionally assists or encourages commission of a crime with the required culpability.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Felony murder::A participant causes a killing during and in furtherance of an enumerated dangerous felony. What homicide doctrine applies?::Felony murder may impose murder liability for qualifying killings tied to specified felonies, subject to limitations.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Voluntary manslaughter::An intentional killing follows legally adequate provocation in the heat of passion without cooling time. What mitigation may apply?::Adequate provocation and heat of passion can mitigate an intentional killing from murder to voluntary manslaughter.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Involuntary manslaughter::A driver recklessly disregards a grave unjustifiable risk and unintentionally kills someone. What offense may apply?::Criminal recklessness or gross negligence causing death can support involuntary manslaughter under relevant law.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Self-defense::A person reasonably believes deadly force is immediately needed to stop a deadly attack. Which justification applies?::Reasonably necessary force may be justified against an imminent unlawful threat, with limits on deadly force.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Necessity::A stranded driver takes an unattended vehicle to escape an imminent natural disaster when no safe option exists. Which defense might apply?::Necessity can justify a lesser harm to prevent a greater imminent harm where legal requirements are met.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Larceny::A thief takes another's wallet without permission intending permanent deprivation. Which theft offense fits?::Larceny traditionally requires trespassory taking and carrying away another's personal property with intent to deprive permanently.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Embezzlement::An employee lawfully holds company cash then fraudulently converts it to personal use. Which offense fits?::Embezzlement is fraudulent conversion of property by someone already in lawful possession.

Criminal Law and Procedure::False pretenses::A fraudster lies to obtain legal title to a car from a deceived seller. What offense fits?::False pretenses involves obtaining title to another's property through intentional material misrepresentation.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Robbery::A thief uses immediate force to seize a purse from the victim's person. Which offense applies?::Robbery is generally larceny from another's person or presence by force or intimidation.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Common-law burglary::A person breaks into another's dwelling at night intending to commit a felony inside. What offense fits?::Common-law burglary requires breaking and entering another's dwelling at night with intent to commit a felony.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Search-warrant probable cause::Officers show a fair probability that evidence will be found in a specified house. What level supports a search warrant?::A warrant ordinarily needs probable cause, a neutral magistrate, and particularity.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Terry stop::An officer briefly detains a pedestrian based on articulable facts suggesting crime is afoot. What standard permits the stop?::A brief investigative stop may be supported by reasonable suspicion based on specific articulable facts.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Miranda warnings::Police question a suspect in custody in a way likely to elicit incriminating responses without warnings. Which doctrine applies?::Miranda warnings generally protect against use of unwarned custodial interrogation in the prosecution's case-in-chief.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Sixth Amendment counsel::After formal charge, officers deliberately elicit statements about the charged crime without waiver or counsel. Which protection applies?::The offense-specific Sixth Amendment counsel right attaches after formal adversary proceedings begin.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Automobile exception::Police have probable cause that a car contains stolen items and search compartments capable of hiding them. Which exception applies?::Probable cause permits a warrantless vehicle search within the scope of the objects sought, subject to law.

Criminal Law and Procedure::Double-jeopardy attachment::A jury in a criminal trial is empaneled and sworn. What rule becomes relevant?::Jeopardy normally attaches when the jury is sworn in a jury trial.

Evidence::Relevance under Rule 401::A photo makes an important disputed fact slightly more probable. Which threshold rule applies?::Evidence is relevant if it has any tendency to make a consequential fact more or less probable.

Evidence::Rule 403 balancing::A gruesome exhibit has minor probative value greatly outweighed by unfair prejudice. What rule may exclude it?::A judge may exclude relevant evidence if specified dangers substantially outweigh its probative value.

Evidence::Character propensity prohibition::A prosecutor offers the accused's bad temper solely to prove similar conduct on the charged occasion. What restriction applies?::Character evidence generally cannot prove conduct in conformity with a trait on a particular occasion, subject to exceptions.

Evidence::Rule 404(b) other acts::An earlier act is genuinely offered to establish identity or motive rather than propensity. What rule governs?::Other acts may be admissible for a legitimate nonpropensity use, subject to other limits.

Evidence::Habit evidence::A person follows the same automatic safety-check routine each morning. What proof may show that routine occurred this morning?::A person's regular response to a specific repeated situation can be admissible as habit evidence.

Evidence::Bias impeachment::A witness owns a financial interest in the company whose conduct is on trial. What impeachment method fits?::Evidence of bias, interest, or motive is generally admissible to attack credibility.

Evidence::Hearsay definition::A witness quotes an out-of-court statement to prove that what the statement said was true. What rule is triggered?::Hearsay is generally an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of its assertion.

Evidence::Opposing-party statement::A plaintiff offers the defendant's own statement against that defendant. How is it treated?::Qualifying statements of an opposing party are treated as not hearsay under Rule 801(d)(2).

Evidence::Present-sense impression::A bystander says 'The car is turning left' while watching it happen. Which exception fits?::A present-sense impression describes or explains an event while or immediately after the declarant perceives it.

Evidence::Excited utterance::A shaken passenger immediately blurts out the cause of a frightening collision. What exception fits?::An excited utterance relates to a startling event while the speaker remains under its stress.

Evidence::Dying declaration::A dying victim believing death imminent identifies the attacker in a homicide case. What exception may apply?::A dying declaration about the cause or circumstances of impending death may be admitted in certain cases.

Evidence::Business records::A store routinely maintains timely sales ledgers through employees with knowledge. Which exception fits?::Qualifying records of regularly conducted activity may be admitted under Rule 803(6) with proper foundation.

Evidence::Statements for medical treatment::A patient tells a physician when symptoms began to aid diagnosis. Which exception fits?::Statements reasonably pertinent to medical diagnosis or treatment may qualify under Rule 803(4).

Evidence::Prior inconsistent sworn statement::A trial witness contradicts an earlier deposition statement given under oath. Which evidentiary rule may allow substantive use?::A prior inconsistent statement given under oath at a trial, hearing, or deposition can be substantive nonhearsay.

Evidence::Recorded recollection::A witness once knew a detail, cannot now remember it, and adopted an accurate note while memory was fresh. What exception fits?::Rule 803(5) allows qualifying recorded recollection to be read into evidence when its foundation is met.

Evidence::Refreshing recollection::A witness consults a calendar to jog memory, then testifies from renewed personal knowledge. What method is used?::Rule 612 permits writings to refresh a witness's present memory, with safeguards for the other party.

Evidence::Attorney-client privilege::A client privately confides facts to an attorney solely to obtain legal advice. Which privilege may apply?::Confidential communications made to obtain or provide legal advice generally may be privileged.

Evidence::Lay opinion testimony::A neighbor testifies that a car sounded unusually loud, based on hearing it. Which opinion rule applies?::Lay opinion may be based on personal perception if helpful and not based on specialized expertise.

Evidence::Expert reliability screening::An expert offers a scientific conclusion based on unreliable methods. Which admissibility rule applies?::Rule 702 requires helpful expert testimony supported by sufficient facts, reliable methods, and reliable application.

Evidence::Confrontation Clause::A testimonial police interview is offered against a criminal defendant without a chance to cross-examine its absent speaker. What protection applies?::Testimonial hearsay normally cannot be admitted against a criminal defendant without unavailability and a prior opportunity for cross-examination.

Real Property::Adverse possession::A possessor occupies another's land openly, notoriously, continuously, exclusively, and adversely for the legal period. Which doctrine may award title?::Adverse possession requires the statutory period and applicable elements of actual, open, exclusive, continuous hostile possession.

Real Property::Fee simple determinable::A deed grants land 'so long as it is used as a library,' with a possibility of reverter. What estate exists?::A fee simple determinable automatically ends when its stated condition is violated, leaving a possibility of reverter.

Real Property::Life estate::A grant transfers a home to Maya for life and then to Jordan. What estate does Maya hold?::A life estate lasts for the duration of the measuring life, after which a remainder or reversion takes possession.

Real Property::Waste::A life tenant intentionally destroys permanent improvements, harming the remainderman. What doctrine applies?::Life tenants must avoid legally prohibited waste that harms holders of future interests.

Real Property::Joint-tenancy severance::One joint tenant conveys her full share to a stranger during life. What happens to that share's survivorship?::An inter vivos conveyance generally severs the joint tenancy as to the conveyed interest.

Real Property::Tenancy in common::One of two tenants in common dies leaving a will. How does the deceased owner's share pass?::Tenancy in common has no survivorship; an owner's share descends to heirs or devisees.

Real Property::Race recording statute::A land purchaser records first in a pure race jurisdiction although aware of a competing conveyance. Which rule governs priority?::A pure race recording statute generally gives priority to the first to record, subject to statutory particulars.

Real Property::Notice recording statute::A later buyer pays value without notice of an earlier unrecorded deed in a notice jurisdiction. What protection applies?::A notice statute generally protects a subsequent bona fide purchaser who lacked notice of the prior interest.

Real Property::Race-notice recording statute::A later buyer pays value without notice and records before the earlier grantee. What rule may protect the buyer?::A race-notice statute generally requires taking without notice and recording first.

Real Property::Inquiry notice::A buyer observes an obvious driveway used by neighbors but never investigates their rights. What type of notice may arise?::Visible facts can place a reasonable purchaser on inquiry, charging notice of what reasonable investigation reveals.

Real Property::Easement by necessity::A landowner splits a tract leaving a parcel landlocked and without reasonable access. What easement may arise?::An easement by necessity can arise from severance of commonly owned land creating necessary access.

Real Property::Prescriptive easement::A neighbor openly and adversely uses a path continuously for the statutory period. Which doctrine may create use rights?::A prescriptive easement arises from qualifying open, notorious, adverse, continuous use for the statutory period.

Real Property::Appurtenant easement::A deed grants Lot A a right of way across Lot B for access. What estate benefits from the easement?::An appurtenant easement benefits dominant land and burdens servient land.

Real Property::License::An owner gives a friend permission to park for a weekend without creating an estate in land. What right is granted?::A license is permission to use land, generally revocable unless an exception applies.

Real Property::Equitable servitude::A buyer with notice of a valid subdivision restriction violates it, and a neighbor seeks an injunction. What doctrine applies?::A valid equitable servitude may be enforced in equity against successors with notice, subject to requirements.

Real Property::Implied warranty of habitability::An apartment's serious, unsafe defects make it unfit to live in despite a lease disclaimer. Which protection may apply?::Residential leases often include a nonwaivable implied warranty of habitability, depending on law.

Real Property::Assignment of lease::A tenant transfers the entire remainder of the leasehold term to another renter. What type of transfer is this?::An assignment transfers the tenant's entire remaining leasehold interest; retaining a reversion generally creates a sublease.

Real Property::Constructive eviction::A landlord's material interference forces a tenant to vacate after notice and reasonable time to cure. What doctrine applies?::Constructive eviction may arise from substantial landlord-caused interference followed by timely vacation.

Real Property::Marketable title::A seller cannot convey reasonably defect-free title at closing under a land-sale contract. Which duty may be breached?::A land-sale contract ordinarily implies an obligation to deliver marketable title at closing, absent variation.

Real Property::Delivery of deed::A grantor signs a deed but keeps it without intending it to take present effect. What requirement is missing?::Deed delivery requires intent for the conveyance to take present legal effect, not mere signature.

Torts::Battery::A person deliberately makes harmful or offensive unconsented physical contact. What intentional tort applies?::Battery involves intentional harmful or offensive contact with another person.

Torts::Assault::A person raises a fist causing reasonable apprehension of immediate harmful contact but does not touch anyone. What tort applies?::Assault involves an intentional act causing reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact.

Torts::False imprisonment::A guard unlawfully locks a shopper in a room, and the shopper knows she cannot leave. What tort applies?::False imprisonment is intentional confinement within boundaries without lawful privilege, with awareness or harm.

Torts::Intentional infliction of emotional distress::A person intentionally engages in extreme and outrageous conduct causing severe emotional distress. What tort applies?::IIED generally requires extreme and outrageous conduct intentionally or recklessly causing severe emotional distress.

Torts::Trespass to land::A neighbor intentionally walks into another's fenced yard without permission. What tort can arise without actual damage?::Intentional unauthorized entry onto another's land is trespass even without major property damage.

Torts::Trespass to chattels::A person temporarily interferes with another's bicycle and causes measurable loss of use but no serious deprivation. What tort fits?::Trespass to chattels covers intentional interference causing dispossession or legally significant harm to personal property.

Torts::Conversion::A person intentionally sells another's rare painting, permanently depriving its owner of possession. What tort fits?::Conversion involves sufficiently serious intentional interference with another's possessory rights in personal property.

Torts::Self-defense privilege::A person uses proportional nondeadly force to stop an imminent unlawful attack. Which privilege may apply?::Reasonably necessary proportionate force against imminent unlawful force may be privileged as self-defense.

Torts::Negligence duty::A driver owes reasonable care to foreseeable pedestrians in a crosswalk. Which negligence element is illustrated?::Negligence ordinarily requires a duty of reasonable care toward those within the scope of that duty.

Torts::Negligence breach::A motorist texts while driving and misses an obvious stop sign. Which negligence element is implicated?::Breach occurs when a person's conduct falls below the applicable standard of care.

Torts::But-for causation::A pedestrian would not have been struck if the driver had obeyed the traffic signal. What causation test fits?::Actual causation is often shown if the harm would not have happened but for the defendant's conduct.

Torts::Proximate causation::A negligently spilled oil slick causes a foreseeable nearby vehicle crash minutes later. What limits the scope of liability?::Proximate cause usually limits liability to harms within the foreseeable risks created by the negligence.

Torts::Negligence per se::A driver violates a headlight law meant to protect nighttime pedestrians and injures one in that way. What doctrine may establish breach?::Negligence per se may apply when a safety statute protects the relevant class against the harm that occurred.

Torts::Res ipsa loquitur::A heavy barrel falls from a controlled warehouse window onto a passerby without an ordinary explanation. What inference applies?::Res ipsa may permit an inference of negligence when an accident ordinarily suggests negligence and defendant's control.

Torts::Contributory negligence::A plaintiff partly causes injury in a pure contributory-negligence jurisdiction. What defense may bar recovery?::Pure contributory negligence may bar negligence recovery if the plaintiff's negligence contributed, with exceptions.

Torts::Pure comparative negligence::A plaintiff is 30 percent responsible for $100,000 in proven negligence damages. Which doctrine reduces the award to $70,000?::Pure comparative negligence reduces recovery by the plaintiff's proportionate responsibility.

Torts::Respondeat superior::A delivery employee negligently hits a customer while doing assigned deliveries. Who may be vicariously liable?::Employers are often liable for torts of employees acting within the scope of employment.

Torts::Abnormally dangerous activity::A company maintains explosives creating serious risk despite utmost precautions. Which liability doctrine may apply?::Abnormally dangerous activities can lead to strict liability for injuries resulting from their characteristic risks.

Torts::Manufacturing defect::A sealed blender has a blade that deviates from the intended design and injures its user. What product-defect category applies?::A manufacturing defect occurs when a product departs from intended design, even if the producer was careful.

Torts::Defamation actual malice::A public official sues over a false statement about official conduct. What constitutional standard applies?::A public official generally must prove knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth for such defamation.
